name: Cairbre

attributes.attribute: a male name shared by several Irish heroes
a poet, son of Ogma and the poet Etan
king whose troubles were a satire of Cairbre

sources: OhÓgain, Dáithí. Myth, Legend and Romance: An Encyclopedia of the Irish Folk Tradition. New York: Prentice-Hall Press, 1991, 70.
Ross, Anne. Pagan Celtic Britain: Studies in Iconography and Tradition. London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1967, 100.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text:
Cairbre is a name used in the old tales of Ireland.
Kings, poets, and warriors shared this name.
Some books write it as Carbry and Carpre.

One well-known bearer was the poet Cairbre mac Eadaoine.
He carried the name of his mother.
His mother was Etan, also a poet.
His father was Ogma, the god of eloquence.
Cairbre came to the court at Tara.
A poet had the right to a proper welcome.
Cairbre received a poor hut and a stale loaf.
He judged the king, Bres mac Elatha, to be stingy.
He made a song of blame.
The song raised boils on the face of the king.
A king so marked could not keep the crown.
So Bres gave up his kingship.
The verse of Cairbre aided the Tuatha De Danann.
It did so in the second battle of Mag Tuired.
When Cairbre died, his mother Etan died from the grief.

okr.objective: A repeated male name in Irish legend that marks poets, kings, and heroes.
key_results: The name Cairbre belongs to several stories.
One bearer was a poet and the son of Ogma.
His satire forced king Bres to give up his rule.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore, 2008.
